title: Living Together: Help, Harm, or Neither

scenes.visual: Trunk with gray-green patches; one patch grows, splits into two question marks; question writes in
scenes.tts: Look at a tree trunk or a rock in a Virginia park. Some gray-green crusty patches there are lichens. Each lichen looks like one living thing. But it is a partnership of very different living things, growing as one body. Do living things that live close together help each other, or hurt each other?
scenes.narration: Look at a tree trunk or a rock in a Virginia park. Some gray-green crusty patches there are lichens. Each lichen looks like one living thing. But it is a partnership of very different living things, growing as one body. Do living things that live close together help each other, or hurt each other?

scenes.visual: Two different shapes join and stay together along a time arrow; a bird touches a seed and flies off, crossed out
scenes.tts: Symbiosis is a close relationship between individuals of different species living together. The partners stay together for a long time. A bird that eats one seed and flies off is not in a symbiosis with the plant.

scenes.visual: Cut-away block: bark, green alga cells, blue fungus layer; bracket one body; sugar rises from alga
scenes.tts: A lichen is a fungus and an alga living as one body. An alga is a tiny green living thing. The fungus forms the outside. It shelters its partner and helps keep it moist. The alga makes sugar by photosynthesis. That food feeds both partners.
scenes.narration: A lichen is a fungus and an alga living as one body. An alga is a tiny green living thing. The fungus forms the outside. It shelters its partner and helps keep it moist. The alga makes sugar by photosynthesis. That food feeds both partners.

scenes.visual: Three columns appear: mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, each with two partners tagged benefits, unaffected or harmed
scenes.tts: Scientists sort symbiosis by what each partner gains or loses. In mutualism, all the partners benefit, like the fungus and alga in a lichen. In commensalism, one partner benefits and the others are unaffected. A lichen on tree bark gets a place to live, and the tree seems unaffected. In parasitism, one partner benefits and the others are harmed.

scenes.visual: Tick on a deer block, blood drops flow to tick; parasite and host tags; time bars compare parasite and predator
scenes.tts: A blacklegged tick can drink blood from a deer for several days. The tick is the parasite. The deer is its host, the living thing a parasite lives on or in. A parasite usually feeds over a long time, often while the host stays alive. A predator kills and eats its prey quickly.

scenes.visual: Three rows answer the question; kindness chip crossed out; chain of survival and reproduction
scenes.tts: So, do living things that live close together help each other? Sometimes both partners benefit. Sometimes one benefits and the other is unaffected. Sometimes one is harmed. Partners do not choose to be kind. A relationship carries on because partners that lived this way survived and reproduced.
